fields.label: Footnote
paragraphs: Showing 6 of 6 entries. How long a rig seal lasts is a question of compression set, not of a cycle count. A compression seal fails when it has taken enough permanent set that it no longer fills the bead seat — not after a counted number of closings. Compression set is measured to ASTM D395 and ISO 815-1, both of which we run in-house. Tell us the rig, the pressure and the duty and we will state the compression set of the compound we propose, so the replacement interval is yours to calculate rather than ours to promise. Values are typical for the rim band and are not a specification for a particular part; see our technical disclaimer.
leads: How long a rig seal lasts is a question of compression set, not of a cycle count.
fields.note: 108 words · live is 26 · the longest footnote in the set and the one carrying the most weight. It replaces three cycle-life figures with the mechanism behind them, names two test standards that are on Margo’s own in-house list rather than at the partner laboratory, and closes with an offer no competitor in this niche is making. This paragraph is what lifts the rubric cap on the section

notes: Real <table> markup with <caption>Alloy wheel rim sizes, leak-test pressures and sealing compounds</caption> and scope="col" on every header. All six rows in the DOM at first paint; filter with CSS, never unmount.

The footnote is the AEO surface and it is unusually strong. “How long does a leak test seal last?” has no good answer published anywhere by a manufacturer, and this paragraph gives one with a mechanism and two named standards. It should have its own <h3> if the design allows: How long a rig seal lasts.

Naming ASTM D395 and ISO 815-1 is the credibility move, and unlike the fatigue standards named on the bellows page, these two are run in-house. That is a materially stronger claim and the copy should say so — it does.

fields.label: Intro
paragraphs: A rig seal is chosen for two things: what the rig runs on, and how well the compound recovers after being held compressed. Air and water rigs take EPDM; a line where oil, coolant or release agent reaches the seal takes nitrile. Name the medium and we will tell you which to specify.
leads: what the rig runs on, and how well the compound recovers after being held compressed.
fields.note: 53 words · live is 27 · the live intro asks for “medium, temperature, and pressure class”, which is the flange-gasket intro rendered unchanged — a wheel rig has a test pressure but no pressure class. The replacement names the two axes that actually apply and answers the common case in the same breath

fields.label: Panels ×8
rows: Ethylene propylene diene rubber, and the default for a wheel leak-test rig. Excellent water, steam and ozone resistance, and it holds its recovery through repeated closings on an air or water line. Not for petroleum oils — if oil or release agent reaches the seal, specify nitrile instead.

Nitrile butadiene rubber, the general-purpose industry standard. Outstanding resistance to petroleum oils and hydraulic fluids — the compound for a rig on a machining or casting line where the wheel arrives with oil or release agent still on it.

Polychloroprene. Balanced across weather, ozone and moderate oil at once, which suits a rig that sits in an open bay or handles wheels from more than one line. Also the family we reach for when flame retardancy is specified.
Polyisoprene. The highest resilience of the eight — it recovers its profile faster between closings than anything else here, which matters on a fast-cycling rig. Not for oil, fuel or sustained heat.

Vinyl methyl silicone, the widest service range of the eight and very good compression-set recovery. Poor abrasion and tear resistance, though — on a seal that a rim edge drags across on every cycle it will not last, so specify it only where the rig is hot and the contact is clean.
Styrene butadiene rubber. Abrasion resistance at low cost, for water-only rigs where the seal is a high-turnover consumable and the priority is price per piece. Not for oil or fuel contact.

Ethylene acrylic elastomer. Our signature compound, supplied to Mahindra & Mahindra for engine and transmission applications. On a rig it is a specialist answer — a hot line where oil is present and neither EPDM nor nitrile holds.

Fluorocarbon rubber, the first choice for aggressive chemical environments. On a wheel rig it is rarely justified — it appears here because we mould it, and because a rig testing castings against a solvent occasionally needs it.
fields.note: Eight panels. EPDM and NBR lead, matching the table above and the two compounds the page actually sells. The silicone panel is the one worth reading — it is honest about a real trade-off, saying that silicone has excellent compression-set recovery but will not survive rim drag, which is exactly the mistake a rig engineer would otherwise make after reading the footnote in section 02. Every range matches the homepage compound table. Each body closes on this page’s own application rather than the generic sealing copy that renders on ten other categories

The silicone caveat is the trust signal.
